title: Closing Helene's Case, Then: How Small Can a Sukkah Be?
subtitle: The kitoniyyot resolution, then Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree about a sukkah's minimum footprint.
sources: Gemara text: Sefaria (William Davidson Edition). Structure and quiz questions 1-2 cross-checked against the Dafyomi Advancement Forum (dafyomi.co.il) overview, points-to-ponder, Tosfos summary, and quiz for Sukkah 3. Tosfos: dafyomi.co.il's "Point by Point Summary of Tosfos" (Yaakov Montrose, Kollel Iyun Hadaf).
before: 2b ended mid-thought on whether Rabbi Yoshiya's opinion (walls reaching the sechach) actually fits Queen Helene's sukkah. This amud closes that out — then pivots to a new question entirely: how small can a kosher sukkah actually be?

A second dispute follows right behind it, only loosely about sukkah at all — the Gemara asks what makes any structure legally count as a "house," and spends real time on it before circling back to the main topic.

flow.label: Gemara closes the Helene case
flow.sub: her sons sat in the main sukkah; she used small side-rooms ("kitoniyyot") for privacy — so it proves nothing either way about a small sukkah's height limit

flow.label: New question: how small can a kosher sukkah be?
flow.sub: Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak rules like Beit Shammai — a rare exception

items.label: Beit Shammai
items.sub: must hold his head, most of his body, and his table

items.label: Beit Hillel
items.sub: head and most of the body only — table not required

flow.label: Gemara tests whether this is really about size at all
flow.sub: or about where a person sits in a large sukkah, with his table left inside the house

flow.label: Resolved: they disagree about both
flow.sub: the minimum footprint of a small sukkah, and where one may sit in a large one

flow.label: Tangent begins: what makes a structure a "house"?
flow.sub: a beraita lists everything a sub-4×4-amah structure is exempt from — continues on 3b

flowCaption: One case closes, one machloket opens and gets a two-part resolution, and a new tangent begins.

opinions.who: Rabba bar Rav Adda, then Rav Ashi
opinions.claim: Helene's sukkah had small side-rooms ("kitoniyyot") off a large central room. Rav Ashi refines it further: the dispute is specifically about those small compartments, not the whole sukkah.
opinions.basis: Answers why the Elders raised no objection to what looked like a small sukkah.

opinions.claim: A kosher sukkah must be large enough to hold a person's head, most of his body, and his table.
opinions.basis: Cited in a beraita; ruled like, exceptionally, by Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak.

opinions.claim: A kosher sukkah only needs to hold a person's head and most of his body — his table is not required.
Rules like Beit Shammai here — against the general principle that halachah follows Beit Hillel. When Rabbi Abba expresses astonishment, he confirms: yes, Beit Shammai, and don't budge from it.
opinions.basis: A recognized exception to the Beit Shammai/Beit Hillel default.

opinions.claim: Objects to the assumption: maybe Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel aren't disputing minimum size at all — maybe it's about a large sukkah where one sits at the entrance with his table left inside the house.
opinions.basis: Challenges via the mishnah's precise wording.

opinions.claim: The mishnah says "unfit"/"fit" — not "he did not fulfill his obligation"/"he fulfilled it." That language shows the dispute really is about the sukkah's own status, supporting that it is about size.
opinions.basis: A close reading of the mishnah's exact wording.

script.speaker: Gemara closes Helene's case
script.gloss: The Rabbis hold her sons sat in a full, valid sukkah; she herself often sat in small side-rooms for modesty, and the Elders said nothing because her sons weren't in those rooms. Rabbi Yehuda holds her sons did sometimes sit there with her — and the Elders still said nothing, so a small sukkah over 20 amos is fine too. Either way, no clean proof survives about a small sukkah specifically.

script.speaker: Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak
script.quote: הֲלָכָה, צְרִיכָה שֶׁתְּהֵא מַחְזֶקֶת רֹאשׁוֹ וְרוּבּוֹ וְשׁוּלְחָנוֹ.
script.gloss: The halachah is that a sukkah must be large enough to hold one's head, most of the body, and his table.

script.speaker: Rabbi Abba, astonished
script.gloss: In accordance with whom — Beit Shammai? (Halachah almost never follows Beit Shammai over Beit Hillel.)

script.speaker: Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak
script.gloss: Then according to whom else should I rule? Yes — Beit Shammai, and that's correct here.

script.speaker: Challenge
script.speakerHe: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק
script.gloss: How do we even know Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel are arguing about a small sukkah's minimum size? Perhaps it's about a large sukkah — where someone sits at the entrance with his table inside the adjacent house. Beit Shammai worry he'll be drawn after his table (ending up mostly outside the sukkah); Beit Hillel aren't concerned.

script.speaker: Gemara tests this
script.gloss: The mishnah's own language — "Beit Shammai deem it unfit, Beit Hillel deem it fit" — looks like it's describing the sukkah's status, not the person's. That fits Rav Nachman's reading better than a dispute about minimum size.

script.speaker: Reopened
script.gloss: But don't they also disagree about a small sukkah's size directly? Two conflicting beraitot are cited — one (in the name of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) requires 4×4 amos and mentions "his table"; another attributes to "the Rabbis" a head-and-most-of-body standard, with no mention of a table. The contradiction resolves if one beraita reflects Beit Shammai and the other Beit Hillel — so they do disagree about size.

script.speaker: Mar Zutra
script.gloss: The mishnah's wording confirms this a second way: it says "unfit"/"fit," about the sukkah's status — not "he did not fulfill his obligation"/"he fulfilled it," about the person's conduct. That points to a dispute over the structure's own minimum size.

script.speaker: Resolution
script.gloss: Actually, Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree about two separate things: the minimum footprint of a small sukkah, and where one may sit in a large sukkah relative to his table. The mishnah's text is read as covering both cases at once.

script.speaker: Tangent begins
script.quote: בַּיִת שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת עַל אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת — פָּטוּר מִן הַמְּזוּזָה, וּמִן הַמַּעֲקֶה, וְאֵינוֹ מִטַּמֵּא בִּנְגָעִים, וְאֵינוֹ נֶחְלָט בְּבָתֵּי עָרֵי חוֹמָה...
script.gloss: Apropos the 4-amos measure, the Gemara asks who taught a beraita listing everything a house smaller than 4×4 amos is exempt from: a mezuzah, a roof parapet, becoming ritually impure with tzaraat, and the special sale rules for houses in walled cities — a list that continues onto 3b.

tosfos.summary: Why Rashi's question about fitting seven sons into seven tefachim isn't really a question.

points.label: (a) Implied Question
points.he: מה שדחק בקונטרס לרב חנן בר רבה מה ראיה לרבי יהודה הא אי אפשר לשבעה בנים בשבעה טפחים...
points.en: Rashi gave a forced explanation of the Gemara's proof per Rav Chanan bar Rabah, bothered that Helene's seven sons clearly couldn't fit in seven tefachim. But is that really a question?

points.label: (b) Answer
points.he: דדילמא ארוכה טובא אבל לא היתה רחבה שבעה טפחים ובניה באותו אורך הוו יתבי
points.en: The sukkah could have been very long without being seven tefachim wide — her children sat along its length, not its width.

tosfos.summary: The six places halachah follows Beit Shammai, and how that fits the story of Rebbi Yochanan HaChorani.

points.label: (a) Opinion
points.he: בסדר רב עמרם פסק בששה מקומות הלכה כב״ש
points.en: Seder Rav Amram rules that halachah follows Beit Shammai in six places: (1) our case — a sukkah must hold his head, most of his body, and his table; (2) Menachos 40a — whether a linen sheet needs tzitzit; (3) how many strings; (4) how long they hang below the corner; (5) Berachos 51b — cleaning the table before washing for bentching; (6) the story of Rabbah bar bar Chana finding a golden dove (and a student finding a purse) after following Beit Shammai, versus a student eaten by a lion after following Beit Hillel.

points.label: (b) Question
points.he: וקצת קשה הא דקאמר התם בכוליה פירקין הלכה כב״ה בר מהך
points.en: But that Gemara in Berachos says the whole chapter follows Beit Hillel except for the table-cleaning case — doesn't that seem to exclude "returning to bentch where you ate"?

points.label: (c) Answer
points.he: ושמא משום דב״ה נמי מודו דלכתחילה מיהא עבדינן כב״ש
points.en: Perhaps Beit Hillel agree that lechatchilah one should go back to where he ate to bentch.

points.label: (d) Implied Question
points.he: ועל מה שפסק בהך דהכא כב״ש אין להקשות מהא דאמרינן פ״ק דברכות (דף יא.)...
points.en: Don't challenge Rav Amram's ruling from Berachos (11a), where Rav Yosef says "one who acts like Beit Shammai has done nothing" — proven from the story of Rebbi Yochanan HaChorani, who sat with his head and most of his body in the sukkah but his table in the house. The elders of Beit Shammai told him he'd never fulfilled the mitzvah his whole life, and the halachah follows Rebbi Yochanan HaChorani.

points.label: (e) Answer
points.he: דההיא פלוגתא בסוכה גדולה כדמסקינן דבתרתי פליגי...
points.en: That machloket concerns a large sukkah — the Gemara later concludes there are two separate disputes, and there halachah follows Beit Hillel. Our Gemara concerns the minimum size of a small sukkah, where halachah follows Beit Shammai.

points.label: (f) Question #1
points.he: מיהו שמעתין דהתם תימה היכי דייק מינה דעשה כב״ש לא עשה ולא כלום...
points.en: But that Berachos Gemara is still difficult — how does it deduce "acting like Beit Shammai accomplishes nothing" when the story shows Rebbi Yochanan HaChorani acting like Beit Hillel?

points.label: (g) Question #2
points.he: ועוד וכי צריך ראיה על זה היכא דהלכה כב״ה שאם עשה כב״ש לא עשה ולא כלום
points.en: And do we even need proof that acting like Beit Shammai fails, once we already know halachah follows Beit Hillel?

points.label: (h) Answer
points.he: וצ״ל דאיצטריך התם לאיתויי היכא דב״ה מחמירים מדרבנן...
points.en: It must be teaching something narrower: where Beit Hillel adds a rabbinic stringency while Beit Shammai leaves it at the Torah level, one doesn't even fulfill the Torah-level obligation by following Beit Shammai.

points.label: 1. Proof
points.he: כדאשכחן לב״ש היכא דיתיב אפיתחא דמטללתא דגזרי שמא ימשך אחר שולחנו...
points.en: This is proven by Beit Shammai's own words to Rebbi Yochanan HaChorani — "you never fulfilled the mitzvah at all," meaning not even min ha'Torah. And from Beit Shammai's case, we learn the same applies to Beit Hillel.

tosfos.summary: More consequences of not being a legal "house."

points.label: (a) Observation
points.he: בירושלמי חשיב שאין טובל למעשר והנודר מן הבית מותר ליכנס בו
points.en: The Yerushalmi adds: it doesn't make produce liable to become tevel for maaseros, and someone who vows not to benefit from "houses" may still enter this tiny structure. It could also have mentioned the law of a betrothed girl caught "at the entrance to her father's house" — which wouldn't apply here either.

tosfos.summary: Why a sub-4-amos house isn't fit for an eiruv even according to Shmuel.

points.label: (a) Explanation
points.en: It's not fit to live in.

points.label: (b) Implied Question
points.he: ואפי׳ לשמואל דאמר פרק מי שהוציאוהו (עירובין דף מט. ושם) עירוב משום קנין
points.en: This is true even according to Shmuel (Eruvin 49a), who holds an eiruv works through a legal acquisition (kinyan), not through dwelling. If it doesn't depend on dwelling, why should "not fit to live in" matter to him at all?

points.label: (c) Answer
points.he: לא מיקנו רשותייהו בשביל בית דלא חזי לדירה
points.en: People don't hand over their rights for a house that isn't fit to live in.

points.label: 1. Proof
points.he: ודכוותיה אשכחן התם שמואל גופיה דאמר בית שמניחין בו עירוב אין צריך ליתן פת...
points.en: Similarly, Shmuel himself says the owner of the house holding the eiruv doesn't need to contribute bread to it — because everyone effectively "lives" there — even though he holds eiruv works via kinyan.
